cim: A look at ~1,400 Urban Legend campaigns where right-wing influencers got paid to push crypto policy and Nvidia sales to China after the US approved H200 sales (ModelRepublic)
cim_eredeti: A look at ~1,400 Urban Legend campaigns where right-wing influencers got paid to push crypto policy and Nvidia sales to China after the US approved H200 sales (ModelRepublic)
szoveg_eredeti:
A series of mostly undisclosed influencer campaigns boosted the chipmaking giant — as well as two AI industry dark-money groups.

Explore the data behind this investigation here.

For more than a year, over 80 different influencers on X have likely been paid to endorse and link to a series of largely pro-AI-industry articles, from defenses of chip sales to China to attacks on “AI doomers,” with many posting on other platforms as well. It appears these campaigns were organized through Urban Legend, an influencer marketing company which WIRED previously reported ran similar campaigns. While most of these posts contain no reference to their likely sponsored nature, one disclosed itself as an ad and directly mentioned Build American AI, the dark-money group connected to OpenAI president Greg Brockman and tech billionaires Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz. Other campaigns shared connections to Innovation Council Action, a dark-money group linked to Trump AI Advisor David Sacks, in part by promoting the articles of its Senior Policy Advisor, Jordan Schachtel. Multiple specifically boosted the interests of Nvidia, promoting its letter on open-weights AI, sharing an interview with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and promoting chip sales to China.

I found at least two dozen AI-related campaigns that appear to be run through Urban Legend, a right-wing influencer marketing firm. Each campaign corresponds to a different URL promoted by these influencers. Highlights include articles with titles like “Woke AI Exposed” and “Trump’s latest move to ensure American AI dominance,” referring to the sale of Nvidia H200 chips to China. While there was some diversity to these campaigns, the most common theme was either attacking Anthropic and OpenAI for being “woke” and insufficiently aligned with the Trump administration, or pushing the administration’s line on China and AI chips, including Nvidia’s sales there. The remainder largely argue pro-industry or anti-regulation lines in other ways, with only three promoted articles taking a cautionary or pro-safety stance toward AI. The most recent campaign ended Nov. 10.

Urban Legend seems to work on behalf of an eclectic array of clients, conducting a wide range of sometimes-conflicting influence campaigns across a variety of topics. It does this through a deep pool of influencers, including Donald Trump Jr. and current FBI Director Kash Patel, until both stopped posting Urban Legend links in November 2024. The majority of its campaigns are unrelated to AI. Urban Legend declined to comment.

The influencers aren’t the only ones who appear to have been paid. Several of the articles promoted in these tweets show signs indicating they were likely bought as well.

Four of the five Trending Politics pieces in these campaigns were filed on the site as “Sponsored” or “Sponsored Plus.” Every policy editorial published without a byline in the first two months at Lyceum, which launched in June 2026, was tied to an Urban Legend campaign, with the account’s other editorials rated as being largely AI-generated. Upward News, which sells “native editorial advertisements,” ran a piece with no byline praising the sale of Nvidia chips to China, with Urban Legend’s first link to it created within 2 1⁄2 hours of publication. None of these sites responded to requests for comment.

These campaigns were found by identifying X posts with shortened links that used similar intermediate redirects, presumably for tracking by Urban Legend. According to WIRED’s previous reporting, Urban Legend pays creators per click or action. The exact arrangement is described in more detail in an archived version of Urban Legend’s web-app code from December 2023. This code contains the terms & conditions agreement between Urban Legend and the influencers it pays, stating that Urban Legend operates a program allowing creators to track, generate, and optimize revenue from digital content. Creators “will be paid fees for Conversions… tracked through the means specified by COMPANY [Urban Legend].” One influencer who shared over one hundred Urban Legend tracked links, including AI-related ones, also confirmed the nature of the relationship, posting, “Wanna be a paid influencer?... Sign up here,” alongside a referral link to Urban Legend’s website.

In order to track these conversions (e.g., a click, sign-up, or donation), it seems they use a system of nearly instantaneous link redirects. Such click tracking itself is routine online; what’s notable here is that the tracking is done not by the site the reader ends up on but by an intermediary. Before arriving at the page being promoted, a creator’s bit.ly link usually forwards first to mycreator.studio, a tracking address that carries a code for the creator and the campaign. Multiple features of the link redirection chain make it clear that Urban Legend is associated with the campaign.

In 2022, WIRED Magazine identified a domain used by Urban Legend in its influencer campaigns, exc.to. This domain was registered with the URL-shortening service Bit.ly, and was used to create redirect links in the same way as conventional bit.ly links. Back in 2021, links to the exc.to domain were already sending readers to their final destination via mycreator.studio. One creator who confirmed to WIRED that they had contracted with Urban Legend used exc.to links that functioned in this way.

Separately, many mycreator.studio links subsequently land on pages with tags in the URLs that explicitly name “urban_legend” as the traffic source for that click.

I found over 8,000 such posts redirecting through mycreator.studio, most for non-AI-related campaigns. While the bulk of the operation seems to be on X, influencers also post these links on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, and Truth Social.

This mycreator.studio domain appears to be exclusively used by Urban Legend. As mentioned, many of the redirected links land on pages with “urban_legend” as the traffic source. None mention another source without also mentioning Urban Legend. The mycreator.studio domain was registered on May 29, 2021, and the first Urban Legend link routing through it was from July 27, 2021. Additionally, the archived Urban Legend web-app code contains test links to a server named ul-conversions-dev.herokuapp.com, with these links appearing in the exact same format as links for mycreator.studio.

I reached out to Urban Legend for comment on Tuesday regarding this article, giving context about how the mycreator.studio links could identify their campaigns, and asking for them to confirm their use of the domain. Within one hour of my email being sent, a new domain was registered, bitlicustom.com. This new domain works just like mycreator.studio, with its links using the same format, and its server giving the same byte-for-byte response as mycreator.studio’s, from the same hosting service. By the following afternoon, at least eight new bit.ly links from Urban Legend-linked creators routed through bitlicustom.com instead of mycreator.studio. Urban Legend did not provide comment.

Some links don’t route through the intermediate mycreator.studio site, instead directly going to the final destination. However, these links are still identifiable as part of the same network. The direct links use the same campaign tracking URL parameters: “utm_campaign=” followed by eight hex characters which correspond to the creator and campaign. They also follow the same coordinated pattern, posting a day or two after the article comes out, and some carry “#ad” labels. Additionally, approximately 90% of accounts that posted these direct links in AI-related campaigns also posted Urban Legend links that include the mycreator.studio intermediary in other campaigns. Nearly an additional 6,000 posts were found that did not route through mycreator.studio.
